pages.text:
Introduction
The University of Virginia Autonomous Watercraft Racing Club is the University of Virginia’s
premiere electric boat propulsion competition team. Since our debut competition last year, we have
bolstered our membership to a small yet solid group of engineering students across multiple disciplines.
In this second year of our competition efforts, we had a lot to improve on and explore with our dual
catamaran design. We were determined to improve our planning and decision-making going into
competition this year. The goal was to make informed and calculated decisions on changes we made to
the boat to optimize for the categories we planned to compete in this year.
We had planned to expand our efforts from just the basic unmanned division to one of the
GPS-driven divisions, expanding on our work from the previous year into this arena. That means we
needed a fully autonomous GPS running, alongside our improvements to the boat. Apart from the GPS,
our key goals were to increase our speed, improve internal cooling, and minimize unnecessary weight.
These three goals were all considered at every step of the way, as we optimized the placement of our
propellers, decided on new motors, and reconfigured our electrical systems, along with much more that
we hoped to accomplish this year.
We were very happy to end our competition run last year with a boat that qualified and completed
the course with only minor issues. However, it was clear that there were multiple bottlenecks that were
holding us back. The catamaran was held together by an overzealous amount of aluminum framing, the
internals were clogged and loosely fastened, the remote control system had a sub-par range, and our
cooling system required manual startup. We began the year by taking note of all of these shortcomings
and laying out a plan for what we wanted to focus on with our monetary and temporal budget.
Improvements
Moving from the previous year, most of our systems were already designed for a catamaran hull
design. We are interested in exploring different options such as single and trimaran hull designs, but we
did not have the experience of funding necessary to get another hull design up and running this year,
though we have settled on an option for making new hulls in the future. For these reasons, as well as
generally stability and space, we kept the catamaran hull design for this competition.
Another goal we wanted to merge with our design from last year was a fully functional GPS
autonomous control system. The navigation system is built around GPS waypoint following, supported by
an IMU and an Extended Kalman Filter for state estimation, with heading control executed through
differential thrust steering of the port and starboard motors.
The core waypoint navigation logic relies on standard GPS positioning, which is sufficient to
guide the vessel to a target location under typical open-water conditions. RTK GPS is layered on top of
this baseline to improve absolute positioning accuracy from the typical two-to-five meter range down to
the centimeter level, which tightens path tracking and waypoint arrival precision.
The IMU compensates for brief GPS outages or noisy readings by supplying angular rate and
acceleration data, and the EKF fuses both sources into a stable, continuous estimate of the vessel's
position and heading. A PID controller then translates heading error into a differential thrust command,
independently varying the speed of the port and starboard motors to steer the vessel without a rudder.
This architecture is detailed fully in Section 3.

Design Components and Analysis
The hull we chose was the Bonzi 84” RC hulls for our catamaran design. The choice to use these
hulls stem from cost-saving and reliability considerations for our team. One of the advantages of these
hulls and the catamaran design is the increased weight capacity compared to a single hull design. Last
year, the team was able to easily hold over 60 pounds of payload without issue. The current catamaran
design affords better stability in rougher waters that might be expected in a semi-sheltered river
environment, reducing the risk of capsizing. In addition, the utilization of a catamaran design allows for a
twin motor configuration and differential thrust steering, reducing the need for a rudder with its relatively
wide beam length

Motor Selection

The vessel utilizes two 84" Bonzi classic hulls joined by an aluminum frame. Factoring in the structural
weight and the mandatory 60 lb payload, the vessel has a significantly higher displacement than a
standard RC configuration, increasing its static draft. Because of this added draft, the propellers will be
fully submerged rather than operating in a surface-piercing condition. This fundamental change dictated
our approach to motor selection, torque matching, and propeller geometry. To meet the extreme power
demands of a heavily laden catamaran, we selected a dual-powertrain configuration utilizing two Castle
2535 Sensored Motors (520Kv), one dedicated to each hull.
Operating at a maximum input voltage of 12S LiPo (50.4V), these motors provide a theoretical maximum
unloaded speed of roughly 26,200 RPM (well below the 38,000 RPM limit). This dual-motor setup
perfectly addresses our torque matching and load requirements. Castle Creations rates a single 2535 motor
for vehicles weighing up to 50 lbs. With our total vessel displacement estimated at 98 lbs, a single motor
would be critically overloaded and pushed outside its efficiency curve. By deploying two motors, we
effectively halve the hydrodynamic load per driveline. This ensures that the immense torque required to
spin our fully submerged propellers remains within the peak efficiency band of each motor, preventing
excessive slip, cavitation, or stalling under the heavy displacement.
To manage the intense thermal loads generated under our full 60 lb displacement, we will integrate a
custom active-cooling water jacket fabricated by Austal, tailored to the smooth exterior of the Castle 2535
motors, and for lower-loading test applications, a 3D printed modular fan mount. While this bespoke
cooling solution is necessary for our current powertrain, future iterations may transition to TP Power
motors; the commercial availability of water jackets for that platform would allow us to streamline
fabrication and refocus our research and development resources on other critical vessel systems.

Battery System Design
The main battery system of the boat, driving the propulsion system, is driven by a total of four 6S
(around 22.2V) 20 Ah batteries, with two in series for each of the left and right motor and ESC. These
provide sufficient power for the boat to travel continuously for the duration of the race given the average
power draw of the motors at racing speeds while being light enough to not shift the center of mass of the
boat significantly. Power is carried from the batteries to the ESCs through bus bars, which allow for easier
installment and replacement of the batteries and ESCs. In addition, each positive end has a thermal-based
breaker switch to protect against too much power draw from the motors and ESCs. These switches also
serve as the main switches for the propulsion system itself, and are mounted onto the surface of the boat
for easy access.

During operation, the power draw of the ESCs can cause a noticeable rise in temperature, with
higher temperatures being emitted with more energy drawn from the motors due to higher thrust.
However, in-house testing has shown that the temperature rise will be a significant issue during operation,
which we have chosen to mitigate with an active cooling system using four small pumps, two on each
hull, all of which are powered by one 12V 7Ah battery to draw in surrounding water as the boat moves.
Propulsion Optimization
Propeller pitch dictates the theoretical advance of the boat per revolution, while RPM dictates
how often that advance occurs. To reach our target speed without exceeding the motors' optimal efficiency
bands, we had carefully balanced pitch and RPM. Last year, our drivetrain suffered from inefficiencies
due to simple copper tubing, an unsupported flex shaft, and arbitrary propeller placement, resulting in
torque roll and thrust loss. This year, we engineered a completely upgraded dual drivetrain featuring
extended strut assemblies, brass bullet nuts for improved hydrodynamic flow, and dedicated left-hand and
right-hand oriented shafts and propellers. The dual Castle 2535 motors drive counter-rotating propellers,
neutralizing torque roll and vastly improving straight-line efficiency and stability.

Autonomous Navigation System
The diagram below illustrates the hardware topology of the autonomous navigation system. The
Pixhawk flight controller serves as the central hub, interfacing directly with the port and starboard motors
via electronic speed controllers, a radio receiver for manual override, the vessel power system, and the
RTK GPS rover module. A Raspberry Pi 5 companion computer connects to the Pixhawk over a serial
MAVLink link and also connects to an onboard LTE router, which tunnels all traffic over a VPN, enabling
waypoint uploads, monitoring, and teleoperation, from any location with internet access.

Components’ description
Pixhawk: Autopilot flight controller. It runs the sensor fusion, navigation algorithms, and motor control
loops. It reads from the GPS and IMU, executes the waypoint following logic, and outputs PWM signals
to the motor Electronic Speed Controllers (ESC’s)
Port and starboard motor: Twin electric thrusters. The Pixhawk drives them independently, via an
Electronic Speed Controller (ESC) for each motor, enabling directional control through differential thrust
rather than a rudder.
Radio receiver: Connects to the operator's RC transmitter for direct manual override, safety intervention,
and arming and disarming.
Power system (batteries): Supplies regulated voltage to all onboard electronics.
RTK GPS (u-blox M8N): Provides the vessel's real-time position with centimeter-level accuracy when
corrections from the shore-based base station are received.
Raspberry Pi 5: Acts as a companion computer. It communicates with the Pixhawk over MAVLink via a
serial connection, and serves as the interface to the onboard router for over-the-horizon command and
control.

LTE/5G router: Provides cellular internet connectivity to the Raspberry Pi. All traffic is routed through
a VPN, enabling secure remote access from any internet-connected location.
Internet (VPN): Represents the over-the-horizon control path. An operator can connect to the vessel
through the VPN tunnel to upload or modify waypoints, or to monitor telemetry, without requiring
line-of-sight radio contact.
RTK GPS

The vessel uses two u-blox M8N GPS modules operating in an RTK (Real-Time Kinematic)
configuration. One module is mounted on the vessel as the rover, and a second is placed at a fixed, known
location on shore as the base station.
Standard GPS receivers determine position by measuring the time delay between a satellite
signal's transmission and its reception, which is accurate to roughly two to five meters. RTK improves on
this by additionally measuring the carrier phase of the satellite signals, which oscillate at a frequency of
approximately 1.575GHz with a wavelength of about 19 centimeters. The base station, whose exact
position is known, continuously computes the difference between where its satellite measurements
suggest it is and where it actually is. These correction values are broadcast to the rover in real time over a
radio link.
The rover receives both the raw satellite signals and the base station corrections. By combining its
own carrier phase measurements with the corrections, the rover can resolve the integer number of full
carrier wavelengths between itself and each satellite, a process called integer ambiguity resolution. Once
this is solved, the rover can compute its position relative to the base station with an error of roughly one to
two centimeters under open-sky conditions. This level of accuracy is what enables the vessel to follow
planned waypoints precisely and return reliable path-following data during testing.
Waypoint Navigation Algorithm
Before departure, the operator loads a mission consisting of an ordered list of Global Positioning
System (GPS) coordinates. Once active, the system continuously computes the desired bearing to the
current target waypoint using the haversine formula, compares it against the Extended Kalman Filter
(EKF) fused heading estimate derived from GPS course-over-ground and Inertial Measurement Unit
(IMU) gyroscope data, and feeds the resulting heading error into a PID controller whose output is mapped
to a differential thrust command across the port and starboard motors. When the vessel falls within a
configurable acceptance radius of the active waypoint, the system advances to the next coordinate,
continuing until all waypoints are visited. The algorithm is outlined below:

pages.text:
Differential Thrust Steering
Our catamaran utilizes a Differential Thrust Steering (DTS) configuration, leveraging
independent electric propulsion systems in each hull to manage directional control. This approach
eliminates the need for traditional mechanical rudders, offering several distinct advantages for our current
phase of development.
The steering is governed by the variance in Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) signals sent to the
port and starboard motors. By creating a thrust imbalance, we generate a yaw moment proportional to the
difference in signal. The width of our boat is sufficiently wide relative to our currently set maximum
allowed throttle.
During initial trials and especially during our autonomous trajectory-following tests, we observed
that DTS provides sufficient control authority at our current operating speeds. The decision to omit a
rudder assembly was driven by two primary factors:
●
●

Reduced Parasitic Drag: Removing underwater control surfaces minimizes the wetted surface
area, improving overall hydrodynamics.
Mechanical Simplification: Eliminating servo-actuated linkages reduces potential points of failure
and streamlines the internal packaging of the hulls.

While DTS is effective for low-to-mid-range velocity and autonomous pathing, we recognize its
limitations in high-speed regimes where the hull may require more aggressive control from a rudder. As
we scale the boat's velocity through allowing more maximum throttle and incremental drivetrain
improvements, the integration of a physical rudder remains a planned upgrade to enhance high-speed
stability and precision.

eliminates the need for traditional mechanical rudders, offering several distinct advantages for our current
phase of development.

        The steering is governed by the variance in Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) signals sent to the
port and starboard motors. By creating a thrust imbalance, we generate a yaw moment proportional to the
difference in signal. The width of our boat is sufficiently wide relative to our currently set maximum
allowed throttle.

        During initial trials and especially during our autonomous trajectory-following tests, we observed
that DTS provides sufficient control authority at our current operating speeds. The decision to omit a
rudder assembly was driven by two primary factors:

    ●   Reduced Parasitic Drag: Removing underwater control surfaces minimizes the wetted surface
        area, improving overall hydrodynamics.
    ●   Mechanical Simplification: Eliminating servo-actuated linkages reduces potential points of failure
        and streamlines the internal packaging of the hulls.

         While DTS is effective for low-to-mid-range velocity and autonomous pathing, we recognize its
limitations in high-speed regimes where the hull may require more aggressive control from a rudder. As
we scale the boat's velocity through allowing more maximum throttle and incremental drivetrain
improvements, the integration of a physical rudder remains a planned upgrade to enhance high-speed
stability and precision.

pages.text:
Autonomous Testing & Validation
●

Open water tests: The vessel successfully completed autonomous waypoint navigation across
multiple open-water trials. Once underway, the vessel navigated the entire waypoint sequence
without any human intervention, after the mission began.

●

Path accuracy data: Across ten trial runs, eight produced results rated as fully successful: the
vessel tracked the intended path efficiently and arrived at each waypoint within the acceptance
radius. Two runs resulted in partial successes, where the vessel overshot or overcorrected on turns
but still converged on the target waypoint after the correction. No run resulted in a complete
failure to reach a waypoint.

●

Failure cases:
○ During early testing, the boat's radio link became unreliable at distance, making it
impossible to update or modify waypoints once the vessel had moved out of radio range.
This was addressed by adding the LTE router and VPN described in Section 5.1, which
allows waypoints to be loaded or changed over the internet from any location.
○ Another operational constraint is that the waypoint navigation system requires GPS
coordinates for each target location.
These can be obtained in two ways:
■ they can be measured precisely in advance using the RTK base station and
external surveying,
■ or they can be estimated by the operator by dropping points onto a map
visualization on the base station platform.
The first method yields high positioning accuracy; the second is faster to set up but
introduces uncertainty in absolute position that is proportional to the quality of the map
and the operator's judgment. For missions where precise final positioning is important,
coordinates should be pre-measured.

pages.text:
Mechanical Design
Battery Storage and Safety
Our battery mounting uses battery holders for our batteries; each holder is able to contain two of
our batteries. We designed the structures ourselves, and each one was 3D printed and is made of PLA
plastic. Once printed, two of each structure are attached to the inside of our hull using heavy duty
double-sided tape. Hook and loop fasteners are used to keep the batteries in the structure. Our testing
has shown that this is more than enough to keep our batteries stationary even at high speeds.
Vibration isolation is accomplished by using a rubber damper on the non-drive side of the motor.
The damper is placed beneath the motor and above the floor of the hull, this dampens the vibrations
caused by the motor and reduces the impact of said vibrations upon the boat itself.

Powertrain
Our motors were mounted using aluminum brackets and 3D printed PLA plastic motor holders.
The 3D printed plastic acts as a cradle which the motor is attached to and this part holds the motor and
allows for it to be connected to other parts. The aluminum bracket was cut with a waterjet and connected
to the sides of the hull and then using M4 screws attached to the motor and motor holder.
To ensure shaft alignment, a 6mm flexible shaft was used for our powertrain. This part made sure
that our motor and propellor would be interoperable by giving us a few degrees of flexibility while
retaining efficient power transmission. We still attempted to keep our motor and propellor as aligned as
possible, however if our propellor testing indicated a different optimal propellor placement location, we
had the necessary flexibility to make changes like moving our motor and shaft without having to worry
about micron level precision in mounting. This ability to easily experiment and make changes to
maximize propeller output easily outweighed any efficiency losses from a flexible shaft when compared
to a rigid variety.

pages.text:
Coupling between the motor output shaft and our main propeller shaft is accomplished with the
use of a half shell coupling. This allows us to connect the hexagonal output of the motor to our circular
drive shaft while ensuring that we are able to transmit all of the motors torque.
Our cooling system is made up of pumps in each of our hulls which pump in water from right a
hole in the hull. We have 3D printed attachments for our hull which will catch some of the water right
alongside the hull and direct it into the openings for the hose. This hose is connected to the pumps and
moves the water from the outside of the hull to the water-jackets for our electrical componentry, including
motors and ESCs. This water has the heat from these components transferred into it before the water is
pumped out again. The pumps in this system were purchased; however the water-jackets were custom
made by our team for their purpose.
Control System
For our control system, we are using a Pixhawk using ArduPilot flight controller software
specifically with the ArduRover configuration. Our Pixhawk is connected to our new RC radio controller,
allowing for improved sensitivity for the controls compared to the previous year’s joystick controller. We
have made changes to improve the signal range of the radio, such as elevating the radio receiver above the
waterproof enclosure box. This helps to reduce the impact of interference caused by signals hitting the
water or line of sight issues. We have also implemented a new cellular router, which should give us
improved coverage at longer distances allowing us to connect to the boat from significantly farther away.
Finally, our initial autonomy system leverages the PID controller in Ardupilot for waypoint control, which
allows our craft to operate on its trajectory even if the signal is lost.

Testing and Safety Procedures
Our testing was extensive this year, one of our main goals as a team this year was to be able to
test earlier in the season as well as more often. This was a goal we achieved and our more extensive
testing regime gave us a much greater understanding of how our various systems operated together while
teaching us about dealing with minor repairs and fixes on the fly.
Our electrical testing regime consisted of powering our boat’s electrical system and ensuring that
all components were operating as expected. This was a fairly common test, being performed every week,
on average. This allowed us to ensure the integrity of our electronic components whenever any kind of
change was made. This allowed the team to capture deviations from our expectations early and fix them
before anything serious occurred, for example making sure voltages were correct or checking electrical
connections.
Dry testing was also performed regularly, generally once every one or two weeks. Our testing
involved securing the hulls or just the motors, if they were being tested outside the hull, and turning on
power before connecting our controller. The motors would then both be powered, slowly increasing the
speed. Then our differential thrust steering would be tested. This allowed us to verify motor and controller
behavior as well as verify instrumentation data readings.
Load testing was performed directly alongside our water trials, before we began every one of our
water trials we performed a load test. This involved fixing the front end of the watercraft and powering up
our motors. We then modulated the power throughout the entire possible range to test motor performance
and measure the thrust to make sure it was within the expected range. This testing regime also allowed us
to test our cooling performance by running our motors under a “real-world” load and then observing our
temperature over time. This allowed us to figure out the most optimal power range for our motors to
ensure maximum speed while not risking overheating.

10

pages.text:
We performed water trials on 10/26, 10/31, and 11/23 with multiple more trials planned in the
lead up to the PEP26 competition. Our trials were performed at Chris Greene Lake, a lake close to our
university, and in the Freemason harbor in Norfolk, VA. These trials gave us tests that most closely
resembled what the PEP26 competition will be like and allowed us to directly test our boat’s performance,
this was where we were able to trial our watercraft’s autonomy system and ensure that it worked under
real-world conditions.

Risk Assessment & Mitigation
Technical Risks and Mitigations
Many of the risks of the boat arise from the propulsion system hardware. This includes significant
risks such as motor overheating, ESC thermal shutdown, and water intrusion, moderate risks such as shaft
misalignment, and mild risks such as prop cavitation. The thermal risks are the most significant because
they can cause immediate and fast-acting destruction of the motors and ESCs, causing complete shutdown
of the boat at best and flame generation at worst.
To mitigate these thermal risks, a low-power active cooling system will be implemented to
continuously pump surrounding water throughout the motors and ESCs to curb temperature rise with
operation of the boat. Though the individual components are waterproof, water intrusion has the potential
to short-circuit the entire propulsion system, causing current overload and complete boat shutdown,
especially if the water makes contact with exposed leads in the boat or the bus bars connecting batteries to
the ESCs. To prevent water intrusion, all adhesive junctions on the exterior of the boat have been done
with JB Weld, a waterproof epoxy-like adhesive that has established marine-use heritage. In addition, the
propeller shafts are also designed to not allow water intrusion, and the cooling system has been tested to
ensure proper sealing within the boat. The only major potential port of entry for water is from the top lids,
which are a tight fit and designed to mitigate water intrusion when closed. In the case of thermal overload
due to short circuit from water intrusion or other causes, the two main breaker switches for the boat
contain a thermally-based fuse, which cuts power to the ESCs if a runaway thermal increase is detected
due to high current continuously passed from the batteries into the ESCs, such as in the case of a
short-circuit.

11

pages.text:
Shaft misalignment and cavitation are milder risks during boat operation, as they do not directly
threaten the functionality of the boat. Because of the boat’s reliance on differential thrust for
directionality, shaft misalignment will have a significant misaligning impact on the boat’s direction of
travel. However, this can be easily fixed during the race by bending the shaft back in place. Cavitation is
also a concern for propeller efficiency during the race, but the structural impact to the propeller will be
negligible over the short period of the race and is instead a long-term concern, requiring propeller
replacements and anti-cavitation design optimization.
On the software side, GPS signal loss and communications loss are two risks that could threaten
the performance of the boat. GPS signal loss would cause significant problems for the autonomous and
over-the-horizon competitions, as the boat would lose its primary source of location feedback data, and
communications loss would be detrimental to navigating the boat during the open and over-the-horizon
categories. In the event of the GPS lock being lost entirely and unable to be recovered, the vessel initiates
a return-to-launch-point using inertial navigation, propagating the last known position forward using IMU
data. Inertial-only navigation accumulates position error over time, so this mode is a recovery behavior
intended to bring the vessel back toward the launch area rather than a precision navigation mode. In the
event of total communication loss, in which the radio link and internet connection are both lost
simultaneously, the vessel can be configured to respond in one of two ways: stop and hold its current
position, or execute an automatic return-to-launch-point sequence. Either option prevents the vessel from
wandering.
Race-Day Risks
For race day risks, there are several that the team has identified and addressed.
At the competition, we have planned to handle moderate winds with waves around the height of
our hull. To deal with this, our catamaran has excellent carrying capacity and buoyancy. We also take
steps to reduce the ingress of water through applying easily removable tape to the top of the hull, which
reduces the risk of water entering the hull and causing a short in the electronics system. This also does not
significantly impede the operators ability to quickly shut down the system in the event of an internal
problem.
Another issue that may arise is the risk of debris hitting our propulsion system. During our tests,
one of our propulsion tubes fatigued and cracked, possibly after striking a piece of driftwood or
underwater debris near the shore of the lake we were testing at. We have taken better measures to
reinforce a new set of shaft tubes during our propulsion system upgrade while also slightly shortening the
protrusion length. This shortening of the propulsion tubes into the water should hopefully reduce the
probability of such a collision happening but it also would reduce the magnitude and consequence of the
impact.
One race day risk that we have identified is hotter temperatures, specifically caused by sun glare.
To help mitigate the internal temperature buildup, we take some preventative measures such as covering
our hulls from direct sunlight until the last moment before launching into the water. This reduces the
internal temperature buildup from sunlight, which can have a slight reduction in the effectiveness of
cooling our motors. In addition, we have tested our improved drivetrain with larger motors, which should
reduce our overall risk of overheating especially for the motors. This, combined with a faster speed,
should mean that we are still comfortably within the maximum allowed motor temperatures for at least 20
minutes.

pages.text:
Future Development
Creating a custom hull has been in our design view for the past 2 years. Last year we were too
caught up in creating a working boat to have enough time, but this year with more hands and the ability to
expand our breadth of operation wider, we were able to start real development. The main driver for
pursuing this avenue was the ability to simultaneously drastically reduce weight and customize the shape
of the hull to fit more optimized electronic configurations and have better fluid dynamics with easy CFD
usage based on our models.
To accomplish this, we tested a new vacuum resin infusion process on a scale mold that will be
able to be upscaled to fit any size boat in the future. This process is generally tried and true around UVA,
but in order to cut down costs and make sizing expandable, we are trying a new molding method of 3D
printed parts combined together to make the full size mold.
The process goes as follows:
Design and print mold parts in attachable format, combining together from the interior with a
fastener. Cover the mold in 5-6 layers of mold release wax. Secure mold to smooth working surface
compatible with PVA release agent and fillet sharp edges and contact points with clay or other materials.
Cover the working surface and mold with multiple layers of PVA.

Lay your fiberglass (or carbon fiber) up on the mold, tightly to the shape of the mold. Use tacky
spray if needed. Cover in a large layer of peel ply, and then a carefully placed smaller layer of
flow-media, based on the geometry and how the flow of the resin needs to happen. Part of this setup is
highly dependent on the geometry of the mold, particularly where the input of the resin is placed and
where the vacuum is sucking from. In this example, the vacuum is sucked out from the edges and resin
will be coming in from the top, which seems to work best for this sort of boat shape. Secure all parts and
prepare input and output tubing.

Prepare the vacuum bagging and secure carefully around the edges with double sided tape,
pleating where needed to preserve optimal geometry accommodation. Once bagging is fully secured, pull
the vacuum, and ensure the bag conforms appropriately to the shape of the mold, adjusting the bagging as
needed.

The actual resin mixing an infusion part depends heavily on the type of resin being used, but in
general, consider the total weight of the fiberglass being used, and mix and equal weight of epoxy with
hardener. Then quickly break the bag where the resin insert is and insert the tube from the pot of resin.
Turn the vacuum on and watch as the resin is pulled through. Once the resin is fully pulled, cut the
vacuum, assuming there are no leaks, it should stay sealed, and need to cure for 24-48 hours.

improvements that we have identified are minor adjustments to the propulsion shaft placement and
increasing thrust and efficiency with custom and larger propellers informed through CFD iteration
combined with empirical testing.

additive friction stir deposition. We chose this method since our larger motor diameter does not have
commercially available solutions. Using additive manufacturing for this application reduces the amount of
material needed while keeping material costs to under a hundred dollars compared to traditional billet

Autonomy Improvements
●
●

GPS and communications-denied operation. Integrating additional navigation modalities such as
Multi-Source Reckoning System (MSRS), would allow the vessel to maintain reliable positioning
in environments where satellite signal or radio contact is unavailable.
Obstacle detection and avoidance. Adding onboard sensing and avoidance logic would allow the
vessel to autonomously maneuver around unexpected objects in its path, without requiring
operator intervention.

Closing
This year of work has been great for everyone involved. We made so much progress on ideas that
have been on deck since conception, finally having enough time to get to the meat of things. The
autonomy system combined with new and improved GPS has been working great, the redesign of the
interior with new motors and propellers will boost performance, which is to be kept in check by the
improved passive/active cooling system, and our future endeavors look bright, with many more plans on
the horizon and great progress towards them.
